1→# How to Publish a TPMJS Tool
     2→
     3→This guide shows you how to create and publish an AI tool that will be automatically discovered and listed on tpmjs.com.
     4→
     5→## Quick Start
     6→
     7→1. Create a new NPM package
     8→2. Add `"tpmjs"` to the `keywords` array in package.json
     9→3. Add a `tpmjs` field with your tool's metadata
    10→4. Publish to NPM
    11→5. Your tool will automatically appear on tpmjs.com within 15 minutes
    12→
    13→## Step-by-Step Guide
    14→
    15→### 1. Create Your NPM Package
    16→
    17→Create a standard NPM package with your tool implementation:
    18→
    19→```bash
    20→mkdir my-awesome-tool
    21→cd my-awesome-tool
    22→npm init -y
    23→```
    24→
    25→### 2. Add the Required Keyword
    26→
    27→In your `package.json`, add `"tpmjs"` to the keywords array:
    28→
    29→```json
    30→{
    31→  "name": "@yourname/my-awesome-tool",
    32→  "version": "1.0.0",
    33→  "keywords": ["tpmjs", "ai", "other-keywords"],
    34→  ...
    35→}
    36→```
    37→
    38→**Important:** The `"tpmjs"` keyword is REQUIRED for automatic discovery!
    39→
    40→### 3. Add TPMJS Metadata
    41→
    42→Add a `tpmjs` field to your `package.json` with your tool's metadata. There are three tiers:
    43→
    44→#### Tier 1: Minimal (Required Fields Only)
    45→
    46→The bare minimum to get listed:
    47→
    48→```json
    49→{
    50→  "tpmjs": {
    51→    "category": "text-analysis",
    52→    "description": "A concise description of what your tool does"
    53→  }
    54→}
    55→```
    56→
    57→**Required fields:**
    58→- `category` - One of: `text-analysis`, `code-generation`, `data-processing`, `image-generation`, `audio-processing`, `search`, `integration`, `other`
    59→- `description` - Clear description of what the tool does (1-3 sentences)
    60→
    61→#### Tier 2: Basic (Recommended)
    62→
    63→Add parameter and return type information:
    64→
    65→```json
    66→{
    67→  "tpmjs": {
    68→    "category": "text-analysis",
    69→    "description": "Analyzes sentiment in text and returns a score",
    70→    "parameters": [
    71→      {
    72→        "name": "text",
    73→        "type": "string",
    74→        "description": "The text to analyze",
    75→        "required": true
    76→      },
    77→      {
    78→        "name": "language",
    79→        "type": "string",
    80→        "description": "Language code (e.g., 'en', 'es')",
    81→        "required": false,
    82→        "default": "en"
    83→      }
    84→    ],
    85→    "returns": {
    86→      "type": "SentimentResult",
    87→      "description": "Object containing score (-1 to 1) and label (positive/negative/neutral)"
    88→    }
    89→  }
    90→}
    91→```
    92→
    93→#### Tier 3: Rich (Full Documentation)
    94→
    95→Complete metadata for maximum visibility:
    96→
    97→```json
    98→{
    99→  "tpmjs": {
   100→    "category": "text-analysis",
   101→    "description": "Advanced sentiment analysis with emotion detection",
   102→    "parameters": [
   103→      {
   104→        "name": "text",
   105→        "type": "string",
   106→        "description": "The text to analyze",
   107→        "required": true
   108→      },
   109→      {
   110→        "name": "language",
   111→        "type": "string",
   112→        "description": "Language code",
   113→        "required": false,
   114→        "default": "en"
   115→      },
   116→      {
   117→        "name": "includeEmotions",
   118→        "type": "boolean",
   119→        "description": "Whether to include emotion breakdown",
   120→        "required": false,
   121→        "default": false
   122→      }
   123→    ],
   124→    "returns": {
   125→      "type": "SentimentResult",
   126→      "description": "Object with score, label, and optional emotions array"
   127→    },
   128→    "env": [
   129→      {
   130→        "name": "SENTIMENT_API_KEY",
   131→        "description": "API key for sentiment analysis service",
   132→        "required": true
   133→      }
   134→    ],
   135→    "frameworks": ["vercel-ai", "langchain"],
   136→    "aiAgent": {
   137→      "useCase": "Use this tool when users need to analyze sentiment in text, detect emotions, or understand the tone of customer feedback, reviews, or social media posts.",
   138→      "limitations": "Only supports English and Spanish. Maximum 10,000 characters per request.",
   139→      "examples": [
   140→        "Analyze customer review sentiment",
   141→        "Detect emotions in user feedback",
   142→        "Monitor social media sentiment"
   143→      ]
   144→    }
   145→  }
   146→}
   147→```
   148→
   149→### 4. Implement Your Tool
   150→
   151→Write your tool's implementation. Here's the example from `@tpmjs/createblogpost`:
   152→
   153→```typescript
   154→// src/index.ts
   155→export interface BlogPostOptions {
   156→  title: string;
   157→  author: string;
   158→  content: string;
   159→  tags?: string[];
   160→  format?: 'markdown' | 'mdx';
   161→  excerpt?: string;
   162→}
   163→
   164→export interface BlogPost {
   165→  frontmatter: {
   166→    title: string;
   167→    author: string;
   168→    date: string;
   169→    tags: string[];
   170→    excerpt?: string;
   171→    slug: string;
   172→    wordCount: number;
   173→    readingTime: number;
   174→  };
   175→  content: string;
   176→  formattedOutput: string;
   177→}
   178→
   179→export async function createBlogPost(options: BlogPostOptions): Promise<BlogPost> {
   180→  // Your implementation here
   181→  const { title, author, content, tags = [], format = 'markdown', excerpt } = options;
   182→
   183→  // Validate inputs
   184→  if (!title || !author || !content) {
   185→    throw new Error('Title, author, and content are required');
   186→  }
   187→
   188→  // Process and return result
   189→  return {
   190→    frontmatter: { /* ... */ },
   191→    content,
   192→    formattedOutput: '...'
   193→  };
   194→}
   195→
   196→export default createBlogPost;
   197→```
   198→
   199→### 5. Build and Publish
   200→
   201→Build your package and publish to NPM:
   202→
   203→```bash
   204→# Build your package
   205→npm run build
   206→
   207→# Publish to NPM
   208→npm publish --access public
   209→```
   210→
   211→### 6. Verification
   212→
   213→Your tool will be automatically discovered through:
   214→
   215→1. **Keyword Search** - Runs every 15 minutes, searches NPM for `"tpmjs"`
   216→2. **Changes Feed** - Monitors NPM publishes in real-time (every 2 minutes)
   217→
   218→After publishing, your tool should appear on https://tpmjs.com within 15 minutes!
   219→
   220→You can verify by searching (requires API key):
   221→```bash
   222→curl "https://tpmjs.com/api/tools?q=yourpackagename" \
   223→  -H "Authorization: Bearer tpmjs_sk_your_api_key_here"
   224→```
   225→
   226→## Real Example: @tpmjs/createblogpost
   227→
   228→Here's the complete `package.json` from the published example:
   229→
   230→```json
   231→{
   232→  "name": "@tpmjs/createblogpost",
   233→  "version": "0.2.0",
   234→  "description": "A tool for creating structured blog posts with AI-generated content",
   235→  "type": "module",
   236→  "keywords": ["tpmjs", "blog", "content", "ai", "writing"],
   237→  "exports": {
   238→    ".": {
   239→      "types": "./dist/index.d.ts",
   240→      "default": "./dist/index.js"
   241→    }
   242→  },
   243→  "files": ["dist"],
   244→  "scripts": {
   245→    "build": "tsup",
   246→    "dev": "tsup --watch",
   247→    "type-check": "tsc --noEmit"
   248→  },
   249→  "publishConfig": {
   250→    "access": "public"
   251→  },
   252→  "repository": {
   253→    "type": "git",
   254→    "url": "https://github.com/ajaxdavis/tpmjs.git",
   255→    "directory": "packages/tools/createBlogPost"
   256→  },
   257→  "homepage": "https://tpmjs.com",
   258→  "license": "MIT",
   259→  "tpmjs": {
   260→    "category": "text-analysis",
   261→    "description": "Creates structured blog posts with customizable frontmatter, content sections, and SEO metadata. Supports multiple output formats including Markdown and MDX.",
   262→    "parameters": [
   263→      {
   264→        "name": "title",
   265→        "type": "string",
   266→        "description": "The title of the blog post",
   267→        "required": true
   268→      },
   269→      {
   270→        "name": "author",
   271→        "type": "string",
   272→        "description": "The author of the blog post",
   273→        "required": true
   274→      },
   275→      {
   276→        "name": "content",
   277→        "type": "string",
   278→        "description": "The main content of the blog post",
   279→        "required": true
   280→      },
   281→      {
   282→        "name": "tags",
   283→        "type": "string[]",
   284→        "description": "Array of tags for categorization",
   285→        "required": false,
   286→        "default": []
   287→      },
   288→      {
   289→        "name": "format",
   290→        "type": "'markdown' | 'mdx'",
   291→        "description": "Output format for the blog post",
   292→        "required": false,
   293→        "default": "markdown"
   294→      },
   295→      {
   296→        "name": "excerpt",
   297→        "type": "string",
   298→        "description": "Short excerpt or summary of the post",
   299→        "required": false
   300→      }
   301→    ],
   302→    "returns": {
   303→      "type": "BlogPost",
   304→      "description": "A structured blog post object with frontmatter, content, and metadata including slug, wordCount, readingTime, and formattedOutput"
   305→    },
   306→    "frameworks": ["vercel-ai", "langchain"],
   307→    "aiAgent": {
   308→      "useCase": "Use this tool when users need to generate blog posts, articles, or structured content with proper frontmatter and metadata. Ideal for content management systems, static site generators, and documentation sites.",
   309→      "limitations": "Does not include AI content generation - you must provide the content. Only formats and structures existing content.",
   310→      "examples": [
   311→        "Create a blog post about TypeScript best practices",
   312→        "Generate a tutorial post with code examples",
   313→        "Format an article with SEO metadata"
   314→      ]
   315→    }
   316→  }
   317→}
   318→```
   319→
   320→## Field Reference
   321→
   322→### Required Fields (Tier 1 - Minimal)
   323→
   324→| Field | Type | Description |
   325→|-------|------|-------------|
   326→| `category` | string | Tool category (see categories below) |
   327→| `description` | string | Clear description (1-3 sentences) |
   328→
   329→### Optional Fields (Tier 2 - Basic)
   330→
   331→| Field | Type | Description |
   332→|-------|------|-------------|
   333→| `parameters` | array | Array of parameter objects |
   334→| `returns` | object | Return type information |
   335→
   336→### Optional Fields (Tier 3 - Rich)
   337→
   338→| Field | Type | Description |
   339→|-------|------|-------------|
   340→| `env` | array | Required environment variables |
   341→| `frameworks` | array | Compatible frameworks |
   342→| `aiAgent` | object | AI agent integration info |
   343→
   344→### Categories
   345→
   346→Choose one of these for the `category` field:
   347→
   348→- `text-analysis` - NLP, sentiment, summarization
   349→- `code-generation` - Code generation and transformation
   350→- `data-processing` - Data manipulation and transformation
   351→- `image-generation` - Image creation and editing
   352→- `audio-processing` - Audio/speech processing
   353→- `search` - Search and retrieval
   354→- `integration` - Third-party integrations
   355→- `other` - Anything else
   356→
   357→### Environment Variables
   358→
   359→If your tool requires environment variables:
   360→
   361→```json
   362→"env": [
   363→  {
   364→    "name": "OPENAI_API_KEY",
   365→    "description": "API key for OpenAI services",
   366→    "required": true
   367→  },
   368→  {
   369→    "name": "API_ENDPOINT",
   370→    "description": "Custom API endpoint URL",
   371→    "required": false,
   372→    "default": "https://api.example.com"
   373→  }
   374→]
   375→```
   376→
   377→## Quality Score
   378→
   379→Your tool gets a quality score based on:
   380→
   381→- **Tier**: Rich (1.0) > Basic (0.5) > Minimal (0.25)
   382→- **Downloads**: Logarithmic scale based on monthly NPM downloads
   383→- **GitHub Stars**: Logarithmic scale based on repository stars
   384→
   385→Higher scores = better visibility on tpmjs.com!
   386→
   387→## Tips for Success
   388→
   389→1. **Use descriptive names** - Make your package name clear and searchable
   390→2. **Complete metadata** - Tier 3 (Rich) tools get 4x the base score
   391→3. **Good documentation** - Add documentation URL to package.json homepage or repository fields
   392→4. **Active maintenance** - Regular updates boost download counts
   393→5. **AI-friendly descriptions** - Write the `aiAgent.useCase` field as guidance for AI agents
   394→
   395→## Testing Locally
   396→
   397→Before publishing, you can validate your `tpmjs` field using the validation schema:
   398→
   399→```bash
   400→# In the tpmjs monorepo
   401→pnpm --filter=@tpmjs/types test
   402→```
   403→
   404→Or manually check the structure matches the examples above.
   405→

1→#!/bin/bash
     2→# Claude Code hook: After a successful git commit, prompt Claude to post to Discord
     3→# Runs as a PostToolUse hook on the Bash tool
     4→
     5→INPUT=$(cat)
     6→
     7→# Extract the command that was run
     8→COMMAND=$(echo "$INPUT" | jq -r '.tool_input.command // empty' 2>/dev/null)
     9→
    10→# Only trigger on git commit commands (not amend, not rebase, not merge)
    11→if echo "$COMMAND" | grep -qE 'git commit\b' && \
    12→   ! echo "$COMMAND" | grep -qE '(--amend|rebase|merge)'; then
    13→  # Check if the tool succeeded - use tool_response (not tool_output)
    14→  STDOUT=$(echo "$INPUT" | jq -r '.tool_response.stdout // empty' 2>/dev/null)
    15→  STDERR=$(echo "$INPUT" | jq -r '.tool_response.stderr // empty' 2>/dev/null)
    16→  RETURN_CODE=$(echo "$INPUT" | jq -r '.tool_response.returnCode // "1"' 2>/dev/null)
    17→
    18→  # Only proceed if the command succeeded
    19→  if [[ "$RETURN_CODE" == "0" ]]; then
    20→    # Extract commit info from stdout/stderr
    21→    COMMIT_LINE=$(echo "$STDOUT$STDERR" | grep -oE '\[.+ [a-f0-9]+\] .+' | head -1)
    22→
    23→    if [[ -n "$COMMIT_LINE" ]]; then
    24→      # Output as JSON with reason field so Claude sees it as context
    25→      cat <<HOOKEOF
    26→{"decision":"block","reason":"[Post-Commit Hook] A git commit was just made: ${COMMIT_LINE}\n\nPlease post a brief summary (2-3 sentences) of what was committed to the #tpmjs Discord channel (channel ID: 1442666515425132644). Include the commit hash."}
    27→HOOKEOF
    28→      exit 2
    29→    fi
    30→  fi
    31→fi
    32→
    33→exit 0

Now I have a comprehensive understanding of the TPMJS ecosystem. Let me now think about the install.sh plans. The user wants:

1. A simple `install.sh` to get started with TPMJS
2. Get the CLI on their computer

- Claude Code and Cursor have different MCP config locations, and I need to figure out exactly where Claude Code stores its MCP servers since the `.claude/settings.json` in the repo is project-level, not the actual MCP configuration location.

Actually, Claude Code uses `~/.claude/settings.json` (global) or `.claude/settings.json` (project) with an `mcpServers` key, same format as Claude Desktop. So the `tpm mcp config` command currently handles Claude Desktop, Cursor, and Windsurf, but it's missing support for Claude Code's config file.

For the install script, I'm considering a simple curl-to-bash pattern that installs the CLI via npm and runs an interactive authentication flow to get the user set up.

I could also do a zero-install approach with `npx @tpmjs/setup`, or a web-initiated flow where users pick their collections and editors on tpmjs.com and get a personalized one-liner with encoded config.

The "antigravity" reference is probably a collection from the user's tpmjs.com account since it's not in the codebase. I need to focus on what actually gets people up and running quickly with their collections across different editors.

content.text:
Perfect! I have the complete official documentation. Let me provide you with a comprehensive answer about MCP server configuration in Claude Code.

## Claude Code MCP Server Configuration

### 1. Global MCP Config Location

**User scope** (global, available across all projects):
- `~/.claude.json` — stores user-scoped MCP server configurations in the `mcpServers` field

This file is created automatically when you add user-scoped servers.

### 2. Project-Level MCP Config Location

**Project scope** (shared with team via version control):
- `.mcp.json` at your project root — stores project-scoped servers

This file is designed to be checked into version control so all team members have access to the same MCP tools. Claude Code prompts for approval before using project-scoped servers from this file (use `claude mcp reset-project-choices` to clear approval choices).

**Local scope** (personal to current project only):
- Also stored in `~/.claude.json` but under your project's path

### 3. JSON Schema/Format for MCP Servers

The standard format used in both `.mcp.json` (project) and `~/.claude.json` (user/local) is:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "server-name": {
      "type": "stdio",
      "command": "/path/to/executable",
      "args": ["arg1", "arg2"],
      "env": {
        "ENV_VAR": "value"
      }
    },
    "http-server": {
      "type": "http",
      "url": "https://api.example.com/mcp",
      "headers": {
        "Authorization": "Bearer token"
      }
    },
    "sse-server": {
      "type": "sse",
      "url": "https://api.example.com/sse"
    }
  }
}
```

**Supported types:**
- `stdio` — local process execution (npx, node, python, etc.)
- `http` — HTTP/2 transport for remote servers
- `sse` — Server-Sent Events transport (deprecated, use http instead)

**Key fields:**
- `command` — executable path or command name
- `args` — array of command-line arguments
- `env` — object of environment variables for the server
- `url` — remote server URL (for HTTP/SSE)
- `headers` — optional HTTP headers (for HTTP/SSE, like Authorization)
- `oauth` — optional OAuth configuration for pre-configured credentials

### 4. Adding an MCP Server with npx and SSE Transport

Here's how to configure an MCP server using npx with SSE transport:

**Via CLI command:**
```bash
# For stdio (npx) servers - most common for npm packages
claude mcp add --transport stdio server-name -- npx -y @some/package

# With environment variables
claude mcp add --transport stdio server-name \
  --env API_KEY=your_key \
  -- npx -y @some/package

# With scope specification (project vs user)
claude mcp add --transport stdio --scope project server-name -- npx -y @some/package
```

**Direct JSON configuration in `.mcp.json`:**
```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "my-tool": {
      "type": "stdio",
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem"],
      "env": {}
    }
  }
}
```

**For SSE transport (remote):**
```bash
# If the server provides SSE endpoint
claude mcp add --transport sse server-name https://api.example.com/sse
```

**Via `claude mcp add-json`:**
```bash
claude mcp add-json my-server \
  '{"type":"stdio","command":"npx","args":["-y","@some/package"],"env":{}}'
```

### Important Notes:

- **Option ordering matters**: All Claude flags (`--transport`, `--env`, `--scope`, `--header`) come **before** the server name. The `--` (double dash) separates Claude options from the server command.
- **Environment variable expansion**: `.mcp.json` supports `${VAR}` and `${VAR:-default}` syntax for dynamic values.
- **Windows caveat**: On native Windows, npx servers need `cmd /c` wrapper:
  ```bash
  claude mcp add --transport stdio my-server -- cmd /c npx -y @some/package
  ```

### Commands to Manage MCP Servers:

```bash
claude mcp list                    # List all configured servers
claude mcp get server-name         # Get details for a specific server
claude mcp remove server-name      # Remove a server
claude mcp reset-project-choices   # Reset approval choices for project servers
/mcp                              # (within Claude Code) check status and authenticate
```

Sources:
- [Claude Code MCP Documentation](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp.md)

Excellent. Now I have a complete picture. Here are **3 plans** for an `install.sh`, ranging from simple to ambitious.

---

## Plan 1: "Simple CLI Installer" — `curl | bash` with guided setup

**What it does:**
1. Checks for Node.js/npm
2. Installs `@tpmjs/cli` globally (`npm install -g @tpmjs/cli`)
3. Opens browser auth (`tpm auth login --browser`)
4. Done — user runs `tpm mcp config` manually

**Pros:** Dead simple, 50 lines of bash, low maintenance
**Cons:** Doesn't auto-configure editors, user still needs to know the `tpm mcp config` workflow

```
curl -fsSL https://tpmjs.com/install.sh | bash
```

---

## Plan 2: "Interactive Setup Wizard" — install + editor configuration

**What it does:**
1. Checks for Node.js/npm
2. Installs `@tpmjs/cli` globally
3. Authenticates via browser OAuth
4. Fetches the user's collections via API (`GET /api/collections`)
5. Detects which editors are installed (checks for `~/.claude.json`, `~/.cursor/`, `~/.windsurf/`)
6. Presents an interactive menu: "Which collections do you want in which editors?"
7. Writes MCP config to the right files:
   - **Claude Code**: `claude mcp add-json tpmjs-{slug} '{"type":"stdio","command":"npx","args":["-y","@anthropic/mcp-remote","https://tpmjs.com/api/mcp/{user}/{slug}/sse"],"env":{"TPMJS_API_KEY":"..."}}'`
   - **Cursor**: merges into `~/.cursor/mcp.json`
8. Prints a summary of what was configured

**Pros:** One command gets everything working. Discovers editors automatically. Handles the API key plumbing.
**Cons:** More complex bash (~200 lines). Interactive prompts may not work in all terminals. Relies on `claude` CLI being available for Claude Code config.

**Key insight:** The current `tpm mcp config` command doesn't know about Claude Code (CLI) — it only targets Claude Desktop (`~/Library/Application Support/Claude/claude_desktop_config.json`). This plan would fix that gap by using `claude mcp add-json` directly or writing to `~/.claude.json`.

---

## Plan 3: "Web-Initiated Personalized Install" — tpmjs.com/setup generates your one-liner

**What it does:**
1. User visits `tpmjs.com/setup` (logged in)
2. Web UI shows their collections and detected/selectable editors
3. User picks: e.g., "antigravity → Claude Code" and "web-scraping → Cursor"
4. Site generates a **personalized** install command with an embedded setup token:
   ```
   curl -fsSL https://tpmjs.com/install.sh | bash -s -- --token=tpmjs_setup_abc123
   ```
5. The script:
   - Installs CLI
   - Exchanges the setup token for an API key (no browser auth needed)
   - Reads the pre-selected config from the token
   - Auto-configures all selected editors
   - Zero interaction needed

**Pros:** Absolute smoothest UX. No prompts, no decisions during install. Shareable — you could put this on a README. Works in CI/headless environments.
**Cons:** Needs a new API endpoint (`/api/setup-tokens`), a new web page, and token management. Most engineering effort.

---

## My Recommendation

**Start with Plan 2, design toward Plan 3.**

Plan 2 gives immediate value — someone runs one command and their editors are configured. The interactive wizard is good enough for now and teaches us what people actually want.

But the **killer feature** is Plan 3's web-initiated flow. Imagine a collection page on tpmjs.com with a button: "Use in Claude Code" → copies a one-liner. That's the viral loop — collections become instantly usable.

### Specific gaps to fix regardless of plan:

1. **`tpm mcp config` needs a `--client claude-code` option** — it currently only targets Claude Desktop, not Claude Code CLI. Claude Code uses `~/.claude.json` with `{"type":"stdio","command":"npx",...}` format, or better yet, `claude mcp add-json`.

2. **A `tpm setup` command** — new CLI command that does the interactive editor detection + collection selection. This is reusable whether invoked from `install.sh` or run standalone.

3. **Collection discovery API** — The install script needs to list the user's collections after auth. The `GET /api/collections` endpoint already exists, so this just needs a CLI wrapper.

---

Want me to start building one of these plans? I'd suggest starting with the `install.sh` for **Plan 2** and the `tpm mcp config --client claude-code` fix, since those are immediately useful.

     4→ * API Key Utilities for TPMJS
     5→ *
     6→ * Keys are prefixed with 'tpmjs_sk_' for easy identification in logs/configs.

    10→const API_KEY_PREFIX = 'tpmjs_sk_';
    11→const RANDOM_BYTES_LENGTH = 32;

    13→export interface GeneratedApiKey {
    14→  /** The raw API key (only shown once at creation) */
    15→  rawKey: string;
    16→  /** SHA-256 hash for storage and lookup */
    17→  keyHash: string;
    18→  /** First 16 characters for display (e.g., "tpmjs_sk_abc123...") */
    19→  keyPrefix: string;

    21→
    22→/**
    23→ * Generates a new TPMJS API key
    24→ *
    25→ * @returns Object containing rawKey (show once), keyHash (for storage), keyPrefix (for display)
    26→ *
    27→ * @example
    28→ * const { rawKey, keyHash, keyPrefix } = generateApiKey();
    29→ * // rawKey: "tpmjs_sk_abc123..." (show to user once)
    30→ * // keyHash: "2c26b46b68ffc68ff99b453c1d30413413422d706483bfa0f98a5e886266e7ae"
    31→ * // keyPrefix: "tpmjs_sk_abc123..."
    32→ */
    33→export function generateApiKey(): GeneratedApiKey {
    34→  const randomPart = randomBytes(RANDOM_BYTES_LENGTH).toString('base64url');
    35→  const rawKey = `${API_KEY_PREFIX}${randomPart}`;
    36→  const keyHash = hashApiKey(rawKey);
    37→  const keyPrefix = rawKey.substring(0, 16);
    38→
    39→  return { rawKey, keyHash, keyPrefix };
    40→}
    41→
    42→/**
    43→ * Hashes an API key using SHA-256 for storage and lookup
    44→ *
    45→ * We use hashing instead of encryption because:
    46→ * 1. We never need to recover the original key
    47→ * 2. Users can generate new keys if lost
    48→ * 3. Simpler and more secure (no encryption key to manage)
    49→ *
    50→ * @param rawKey - The raw API key to hash
    51→ * @returns SHA-256 hash as hex string (64 characters)
    52→ */
    53→export function hashApiKey(rawKey: string): string {
    54→  return createHash('sha256').update(rawKey).digest('hex');
    55→}

    63→export function isValidApiKeyFormat(key: string): boolean {

    65→  return key.startsWith(API_KEY_PREFIX) && key.length >= 40;

  // Node relationship
  nodeId      String                    @map("node_id")
  node        WorkflowNode              @relation(fields: [nodeId], references: [id], onDelete: Cascade)

  // Execution state
  status      WorkflowNodeExecutionStatus @default(NODE_PENDING)

  // Input/output
  input       Json?                     @db.JsonB
  output      Json?                     @db.JsonB
  error       String?                   @db.Text

  // Timing
  startedAt   DateTime?                 @map("started_at")
  completedAt DateTime?                 @map("completed_at")
  durationMs  Int?                      @map("duration_ms")

  // Retry tracking
  attempt     Int                       @default(1)
  maxRetries  Int                       @default(0) @map("max_retries")

  // Timestamps
  createdAt   DateTime                  @default(now()) @map("created_at")

  @@index([executionId])
  @@index([nodeId])
  @@map("workflow_node_executions")
}
